utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you understand? An attack by the Mujahedins, you told us that you had been warned that there would be an imminent attack by the Mujahedins and that is the reason why you left your house. What do you mean by that, by that attack by the Mujahedin? What do you have in mind specifically when you speak about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me tell you, at that time, if we were to be afraid of anything at that time, it was an attack by Mujahedin. We knew that there were some foreign mercenaries who were prepared for anything. They could kill or slit throats. So the very thought made us very scared. Also, we knew about something that had happened in Dusina and in some surrounding places at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, Witness, when mention is made to you of an attack by the Mujahedin, you think of barbarians who are going to attack the Croatian houses and going to kill the Croatian civilians. Is that what you had in mind then?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Still, how can you account for the fact that only those Croats living close to the Muslims were evacuated? How do you account for the fact that only the Kupreskic houses were evacuated and not the Zume houses, not either those houses occupied by the Sakic family? It would have been logical to have all these houses evacuated if the attack by the Mujahedin was to come from the north. Isn't that a view you would share with me?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know why those and other homes did not evacuate. I only know what I was told that morning, what information I received. Even earlier, when I had been moving to take shelter, in fact, my brother's house and my own house were the closest to the Muslim ones, and so myself and my family, we had to move out of there because I was scared. I feared that I had to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, if you fear some attack by the Mujahedins from the north, you would agree with me to say that Zume and the Zume houses are the most exposed to such an attack?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I agree that Zume was also exposed to attack, but we didn't know where else to go. I mean, believe me, there was no where else to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know where the attack is going to happen; however, Zume and the Zume houses are exposed to this attack that is feared, and still you don't take any steps, for instance, to have protection of the shelters?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me tell you, in the area where we went after we had left our families in the shelter, near Niko Sakic's house, there were some people there, so that was one shelter. Near Niko Vidovic's house, there were also people. Later, I learned that there were some, but at first I didn't know. I didn't know about any shooting. The Vrebac shelter was in the middle of the Croat-inhabited area, so you had to go through this area to reach it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you fear an attack by the Mujahedin, you think that they're going to attack the Croat houses, and still you remained in that depression, on the eastern edge of that depression, watching what might happen in the Muslim part of the village. Isn't this totally illogical?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We weren't there to observe what was going to happen in the Muslim section of the village. I said, when the shooting started, we ran into this depression. Perhaps it was stupid for us to have done so. Because on one side, we were hiding ourselves, and on the other side, we were still looking to be close enough to the shelters where our families were and where Niko Sakic's house was. We also had control of the path where some soldiers or some other people with bad intentions may come from so that we could protect whatever we could protect if that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know today how many people died in Grabovi and how many houses were torched? Do you have any idea about it?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Today, from hindsight and through this trial, I now have learned how much we did not know. On the 16th, 17th, and 18th, I learned very gradually, and then from stories. A month later, I learned some other things. I did not know until I came here the scope of the tragedy. I knew that the village had been burnt, I knew that the property had been destroyed, and I saw the ghost-like landscape, but I didn't know that until today. Now I can tell about the number of casualties, which I learned here, and I don't know to date whether this is the definitive number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned in the morning of the 18th of April towards your houses, did you go to see what had happened around your houses in Grabovi or did you only go to your house?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On that day, I managed to get to my house. I never attempted to go anywhere beyond that. When I was approaching the house then, I could see the area around my house and the other houses which were burnt down, and I had no need, I had no desire to go anywhere beyond that. This was very brief, and I described how I went over there and how I went back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about your house, saying that it was devastated, that it was broken into. Was the damage noticed officially in some way or another, through repair bills or through statements to have compensation? Is there any such document establishing how much damage was done?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There is no document, nor did I seek to get one. I would have been -- I wish almost that it had burned down because now I don't feel like I ever wanted to have anything to do with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you return into that house to live there?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Ten or fifteen days later, that is, after those events, I managed to move my family to Vitez to my wife's sister's, who did not live in her house because she was living in Switzerland at the time. Until 10 June, they lived there, until a shell fell in, and then this shell fell and hit about ten children. Shrapnel hit my mother-in-law; she held my one small child in her lap. Then after that, I moved my family back and I moved them back to the house in Ahmici. After the cessation of hostilities, I tried to find an apartment, and I managed to get a contract. I got a contract for eight years, and I'm still paying 300 to 350 marks a month, and thank God that I have dealt with reasonable people now because I'm not paying currently. This has been very traumatic for both myself and my family. I cannot just allow myself to live over there in that area right now any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Simply tell us when exactly you returned to live in your house in Ahmici. You said after the war, but could you be more specific as to the date?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, on 10 June, 1993, this shell fell in Vitez and killed ten children. My decision then was, I don't know if it was a day or two later, but this was the reason for my moving them back from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your parents? Where did they live after the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My parents were in Rovna, together with my family, for a few days, and then they moved back into Josip Vrebac's house. His daughter owned a house where the shelter was, and they stayed there 15 to 20 days. Occasionally, they would visit the house, my mother kept some chickens there, and so after 15 or 20 days, they went back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us during the examination-in-chief that in the afternoon of the 18th of April, together with other people, you were taken to Pirici where you had to dig trenches. Then, later on, after digging trenches for a few days, you were transferred to Upper Ahmici where you stayed until the end of the war. Could you be more specific as to the meaning of that? You said that you stayed there until the end of the war, but I suppose that you could go back to Vitez to see your family; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. On the 18th, when we arrived in Pirici, we spent two or three days there, I'm not sure how many, and then we were transferred to this part of Ahmici. At that time, this line of defence, or whatever it was called, was established there. So we dug ourselves in, that is where the trenches were dug, and this is where I spent the rest of the wartime. Occasionally, there were shifts and I was relieved. It was getting more and more difficult because there were fewer and fewer people to man the lines, so 10, 15 days would pass before you were relieved. But occasionally I would come back, and I would even sleep in the house and spend some time with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout that period, did you participate in any fighting?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were very few attacks at this sector of the defence line. I was in a trench all this time. I was not taking part in any attacks; I was defending from possible attacks. This particular area was not attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You showed us a demobilisation certificate, Exhibit D112. Do you also have your military service book, you know, this booklet showing your service and the various assignments you were entrusted with? This is the kind of book you find in any country. Do you have that military booklet?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There should be a military booklet extant. I don't know where it is. I can ask my wife to look for it. It should be around somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you looked for the demobilisation certificate, but you were not able to hand over to us that military book, as was the case with your brother Zoran. Let us move on to the relations you had with Suhret Ahmic's family. Prior to April 1993, what kind of terms were you on with the members of that family, and more specifically, with Suhret?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean Sukrija?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I have Sukrija in my -- Suhret or Sukrija is the name.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that out of Sakib Ahmic's family I was closest with Naser, who was my peer. As regards Sukrija, we were very different generations. We would just greet each other, but we had no particular relations. We did not visit each other's house. I never visited his, and perhaps, when he was small, he may have visited mine with his parents, but I never went to his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't know the house as such, the inside of the house, but were you familiar with the workshop where Sukrija would repair the cars?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was never in his house and never in front of his house. I know that Sukrija was working on cars, because I saw near Zoran's house there was -- he was discarding body parts, auto-body parts, so I knew that he was an auto mechanic, but I never entered the premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're now in open session, so please do not mention any family name, any surname, but I shall ask you, as I asked your brother Zoran, what you thought, what your feelings were when you heard the testimony of Witness H. Do you see who I mean? Or would you like me to show you the name of that witness?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you allow me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what did you think of -- how did you feel when you heard the testimony by Witness H as to the circumstances under which her father died, and her, her little sister, and her mother were forced to leave the house?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me tell you, it was very hard for me. You cannot even imagine what type of situation you can find yourself in when you know for sure that you did nothing, that you wanted everything best for them. I do not doubt that any of this happened to these people. I do not doubt what the child said, except it had nothing to do with me. I couldn't have been there. I wasn't there. It is -- I also want to point out that for six months I was not even mentioned, and then, for reasons unknown to me, somehow I found myself on some kind of a list. At first I was not even mentioned, and that points to this search for names, for then our cursed houses were mentioned, and the only reason I can come up with now is that; no other reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But could you say that the witness had specific reasons to resent you, you or your family?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot say whether she had particular reasons to be angry, to be upset. The relations were not bad so that that would create a basis for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness we are speaking about made a statement in September 1993. This is marked D1, an exhibit suggested by the Defence. During this statement, the witness mentioned you. You remember that, don't you? The witness stated your name to the investigating magistrates in Zenica. She described how things happened, in words that very much resemble those used in the Court, and this happened on the 17th of December, 1993. This girl was then 12 or 13 years old. So we may think that if she made that statement on the 17th of December, 1993, just because she was then interviewed, if she had been interviewed any earlier, we might believe that she would have said exactly the same thing. Would you doubt that she would have said the same things?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have every reason to doubt it, because if you look at the statements given by her mother, you can see what the mother said. And everybody should have some doubts about it, not just myself. The mother said what she had told to her mother, and I was never there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it's the opposite, but never mind. Do you remember what the young girl said in December 1993 to the investigating magistrate in Zenica, but also here, last year, in this court, as to you being in the house, armed and in uniform, and as to the very short exchange you had with your brother Zoran? Do you remember that part of his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I repeat, I was not there. I had no conversation with my brother, nor was my brother with me in that house. I said where we were, and I said what I think about that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that written statement -- I can't remember whether she said that again in court, but she said in her written statement that she kneeled down in front of you to beg you to save her life. Are you familiar with her statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I need to raise an objection. The witness answered the question. He told what his position is, what he thinks about the statement of this witness, and now I believe that it is inappropriate to mention every single bit of the statement. It is just torturing of the witness. He can go down the list and repeat every single detail, whereas the witness has stated his position on the veracity of the entire --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I heard in my French translation I was torturing the witness. I do object to that notion of torture, but I'm glad to move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you meant torturing the witness, but that is a bit exaggerated, I think. The Prosecutor is not torturing the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: My apologies. It wasn't meant to sound as drastic as it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier, please move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you also heard the testimony of [redacted] when he said what happened in his house and he spoke about the circumstances under which the four people living with him in that house died. Among the four people were two children. As I put the question to Zoran, I'm going to put the question to you. What did you think, what was your reaction, and do you have any explanation following such testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can repeat how I felt while the first witness testified, and as regards to this witness, I felt even worse. I never experienced such a trauma. It's terrible. Imagine when somebody charges you, and you didn't even try to -- charge you with anything -- you didn't even try to do anything bad, I mean, they charge you with the baby of three months. Those children played with my own children; those children lived with my own. If those children came to my store, if I gave a piece of chocolate to my child, I would give some to them as well. You know what that means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that if you are innocent, it was very hard to hear such a testimony. What I'd like to hear from you now is some explanation. After all, you are charged with a very abominable crime. I mean, if you are an innocent, of course, it would be something diabolical, and I think this requires an explanation. Do you have such an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you have statements, four or five statements in which I'm never mentioned, and then a year later it seems that I was the one, and after -- and a year later, somebody says that it could have been me, how can one trust such statements? I do not question that event, that it happened, that people experienced traumas and trouble, but it is not my fault. I was not there. Had they been sure that it was me, they would have said that it was me right at the start. But five statements were made, and I am never there. On various tapes, when they give their statements, also, my name never figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to know something else. When you heard [redacted] testimony, did you doubt the fact that [redacted] was indeed witness to the murder of his family?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that. I do not know where [redacted] was, whether he was inside the house, whether he saw all that. I cannot comment on that. As I said, I do not question that it all happened, but how it did happen, I do not know. All I know is that I have nothing to do with that crime. I have nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with [redacted] house? Had you been in the house before?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As a child, with my parents, we visited with [redacted], when I played as a young boy with Naser. I already said that we were peers. When I came out of the elementary school and went to Trstenik, I never once again went, either with my parents, nor was I anywhere near the house, because life just -- I just took another path, and I led a completely different life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know where [redacted], in which room he lived in that house in April 1993? Did you know whether he lived upstairs, or the ground floor, or in the cellar, in the basement? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said that I was friends with Naser and that he had a cobbler's shop at the station. When he would close for the day, he would come to see me there at the wholesale unit. From conversations with Naser, I knew that [redacted] lived with him. I knew that he had trouble with all his children, that Naser had taken him into his house, that he was living with him. I knew that Naser had a small child -- that is, a three-month-old baby; I believe it was three months old -- and I think he treated me to a drink when the baby was born. But which room [redacted] occupied, I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Terrier. Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we may go into private session for just a few moments?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, can you tell us, to clarify the transcript, you answered some questions about the roadblock in Ahmici that was set up after the conflict of the 20th of October, 1992 when you were the first person and Ivica Kupreskic manned the checkpoint from the Croat side. Will you please tell us who were the Muslims at that checkpoint? Do not mention the name of the witness. Give us just the pseudonym and the name of the other person who was with him.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the Croat side, Ivica and I were there, and on the Muslim side was this witness, but I do not know his pseudonym, really --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Z?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I see. Witness Z and Sidik Ahmic, so two Croats and two Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Sidik and Witness Z, did they have any rifles?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it common in Bosnia, when you told us about the automatic rifle, did you mean an automatic rifle which is called AK-47?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard about it for the first time here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you call an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We called it Kalashnikov or we called it Gypsy girl. That was the vernacular that we used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, do you remember Witness C? Do you know who that is? (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you on good terms with his parents or is it your parents who were friends of his parents?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yesterday, I said that my parents were on good terms with most of their Muslim neighbours and most people who were of the same generation, and the same holds true of the parents of that witness. I'm simply not of that generation, and like all those other people who were older, I mean, I had the same attitude to them. We would meet, we would greet one another, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you on good terms with -- you told us that you knew the daughter from that family; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I knew those people and those children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you were not sure if you would recognise that witness at the time and said it is that particular child.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I said that if I would come across a group of children, and if you asked me to identify that particular child, no, I wouldn't have been certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if you had any contact with him? After you saw him there, did you have any contact with him? Did you communicate with him? Were you at a party together? Were you at a ceremony somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was a 12-year-old child. There was nothing that would bring me to contact with him, nor could we appear at the same party together. Only perhaps I played music at some of the parties, and then he would be among the audience or something like that, but otherwise ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this witness testified here, he couldn't remember your name. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, do you remember that he could not distinguish between Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic, he couldn't recognise both of you?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you explain it now, that he is very precise when he tells the investigator who were the persons that he saw at Jozo Alilovic's?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, how he could quote precisely those names, whether somebody told him which names to say or whether the boy was simply mixed up, I just don't know. But I said it yesterday, if I may add, I was never in my life with such a group of people as described by you. I mean, he mentioned two other people also and said that I was with them, but I was never with those two people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that he describes you quite differently from other witnesses who incriminate you here, that is, Witness K says that you had a black uniform, [redacted] says that you had a black uniform, and that boy says he saw you in a camouflage uniform with your face clean, and these witnesses say that your face was painted. Can you explain these discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is just another proof that it was not me, that it had nothing to do with me. I never had a black uniform in my life, nor did I have a camouflage uniform, except during the war. As I said, at times, I would use my brother's jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to these testimonies, very briefly, I shall ask you, [redacted] told the investigating judge in Zenica on the 3rd of December, 1993 that two persons entered his house who looked like Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is what I said. After a couple of statements, we began to look alike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness H, on the 17th of December, 1993, mentioned you here for the first time, even though her mother affirmed that she had mentioned you, just one person?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not in all statements?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, Witness H's mother made a statement on the 20th of December, 1993, that is, three days after Witness H, and she too mentioned your name for the first time, and it is one in the same family. What would you say to that? What is your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that the mother's statements are highly telling. There are three statements where I'm not mentioned, and then in the fourth statement, I'm mentioned, that I had been seen, that I had been walking around the village and mounting guard. But two other relatives of mine and my brother also mentioned in the same light, and only in the fifth statement it is the two of us who were in that house, who had been in that house and done that, that is, only in the fifth or even in the sixth statement. I've forgotten how many of them there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you comment on the fact that they are people from one in the same family? You said that you had absolutely -- that those people had no reason to bear any grudge against you. So why would this family say this about you?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know why that family. All I know is that it is one in the same family, and I said that we had been here together, my brother and I, for two years and that we've been asking ourselves and wondering and trying to understand, and the only reason could be those houses of ours. There were pressures against those people, "Tell us names. Tell us names." People didn't know what it was about. After awhile, with all this pressure to come up with some names, then they began to mention our houses, and they, of course, associated us with those houses. In the beginning, nobody mentioned my name because it was in combination with Ivica, whether Ivica was in Germany or where, so let's put Mirjan there and let him account for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it seem to you that perhaps the idea behind it was that a Croat had to account for all of that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Somebody needs to account for those crimes, I mean, there is no question about that, because a crime was committed and somebody needs to be brought to justice. But if it was committed by Croats, then not all Croats need to be imprisoned, not all Croats need to account for it, because there are people who are not guilty of that. There is no question about the crime being committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, let us see about something else which arose during the cross-examination. Tell me, please, after the 20th of October, 1992, when you left your home after hearing the report that the Muslims, the Mujahedin might attack your houses, where would you go then?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Every time when we received such reports, we would use that same path and go to Vrebac's shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Did you, on any prior occasion, go to Rovna or to Vitez and shelter your family there?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that every time when we left, we used that same path and went to Vrebac's shelter. We never once went to Rovna, to Vitez, or any other place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, ever since the attack of the Serbian aviation in April 1992, when they attacked Vitez, were any shelters planned, envisaged for your part of the village?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For our part of the village, no, no shelters were envisaged, and people had hid wherever they could. In that place, that part in Zume, yes, there was that shelter envisaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you go to the shelter in Zume?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you? Why did you stay?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We stayed there in one cellar or another, in a cellar which was safer, better, if it was worse, but it wasn't all that frequent. I mean, bombing sometimes would come closer, and that was on one or two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Muslim part of the village, if you can tell us, in that lower part of the village which is below your houses, did you ever see the Muslim army by night or Muslim soldiers before the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that between the 19th and the 20th, as some military passed through and stayed in the school, and I said that from Ivica's terrace, we could see. I described their outlines, their silhouettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you certain that in that part of the village, there were no Muslim military on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: How could we be certain about that? I wasn't certain about that and I didn't know if there were any soldiers of that kind down there. We simply did not use that road for those reasons, because we saw the military then, but we were not certain and we did not use that part of the road. We only used the upper road under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, you felt safer in the Croat part of the village; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between your houses and Niko Sakic's house, and we spoke about that, will you tell us, which was the principal reason for you to go there? Was the chief reason that you went there to watch, to be able to see something, to be able to observe the situation in your part of the village, in Ahmici, or was there some other reason for it?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The chief reason was to be in the vicinity of that shelter so if any group headed there, towards that shelter, to try to protect it, and that is why we were there. We had a view of that road which led from our houses to that depression and to that shelter and Niko Sakic's house. That was the chief reason. We had no other reason. Perhaps it was stupid at the time, but we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which one of you made that choice?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, nobody made that particular choice. There was gunfire, and we scuttled into that depression. First, we hid from the gunfire. Of course, we were hiding there all the time, but then instinctively, we simply thought that if anyone would come near, that they would have to use that road, that path. We had no other choice, and the gunfire was the nearest to our houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, you were at war and you spent a year in the trenches. Of course, you had more experience than -- you were more seasoned than you were on the 16th of April, 1993. Was it, militarily speaking, a well-chosen position? Was it a position at all?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was no position. It was simply saving ourselves, our lives. Perish the thought if anyone came near us because they would have got one after the other. It wasn't simply a military position. It may have been very stupid, but we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ready? Were you prepared to fire that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, had anyone started towards the shelter and children, I would have defended them for all I was worth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Will the usher please show you these photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D115/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, could you please take a look? What can you see on photographs 3-5 and 3-6, on the last page? What is this? Which path is this and where does it lead from?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Picture number 3 is the house of Mirko Vidovic, and that is the road that leads to our houses from the main road. That is where the Sutre warehouse was at the time. This path leads this way. It is below the forest that we called Stipanova forest. This path leads from the Sutre warehouse towards the house of Niko Sakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at photographs 5 and 6?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Here it goes into part of the forest, and this is where Niko Sakic's house is. So this path here leads to this one and leads all the way to Niko Sakic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 6, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Number 6 was taken from Niko Sakic's shed and garage, that is to say, this is where Niko Sakic's house, this is where Niko Sakic's shed and garage are, so you can see the path here that leads to the Sutre warehouse, and the other path would fork off this side towards the depression where we were, there (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at photographs 1 and 2 as well, and where does that path lead from?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Here (indicating), this is Mirko Vidovic's house, this path leads to the road, and this is the road up here, and this is the Sutre warehouse. This is where this path would be up here. Up here, it would go up to this road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Down here, on photograph number 2, you can see this path from the houses to --

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the path that goes back to Niko Sakic's, and it goes out here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, we can see it. Mr. Kupreskic, you showed this to us. What's important for me for you to say is that the path that you spoke of yesterday that leads from the main road, this main road that leads through Ahmici then passes by Dragan Vidovic's house and goes down to the depression -- no, not the depression, to Niko Sakic's house, rather, that is this other road, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is one of the paths, but then there's this other road that I spoke of that goes by Dragan Vidovic's house. That is a road -- that's a big road. You can take a car along that road. From Dragan Vidovic's house, it also came to this road, towards Zume. So Zume was completely linked to it in this way, the lower part of the Zume, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This path that leads from Niko Sakic's house to the right-hand side where Dragan Vidovic is or, rather, where Dragan Vidovic's house is, that road was also being used, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Part of the Pudze houses used it when -- that is to say, from the Pudze houses by Niko Sakic's house, by Mirko Vidovic's house to that road that leads to the upper part of Ahmici and then down to the road and to the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That road comes out by Niko Sakic's house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how many people were in the depression on that day, as far as the Croats are concerned, I mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: With me in the depression on that day were Mirko Sakic, Dragan Vidovic, Dragan Samija, Drago Grgic, and my brother, Zoran Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is five people enough to do anything in a military sense?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Five men is not enough at all to do something from a military point of view. Five men would fight if something would happen and if their families would be threatened, and our families were nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you know on the 16th, 17th, and 18th that the Muslims, Ramo Bilic and his family and the Strmonja families, were in the Vidovic shelter?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 17th, we found out that all these families were in the Vidovic shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you pass by on the 18th, 17th, and 16th, that is to say, did you pass by their houses?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Every time I went to see my family, every time we would try to get to the shelter, we would always pass by those houses and by that shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the houses whole?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The houses remained intact until the present day, and I think that these people have returned to live in their own homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know and did you receive any information as to the following: When the dead bodies were taken out of Sakib Ahmic's house?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard perhaps a month later that UNPROFOR had taken the human remains out of the house of Sakib Ahmic. How many persons were concerned, that, I did not know until I arrived here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when this happened? Can you say how much later or do you not remember, I mean, how much after the crime in Ahmici had taken place? Can you determine the date?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I heard about it approximately a month after the crime had been committed. I heard that UNPROFOR had taken them out, but when this exactly occurred, that, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you found out about the indictment in 1997, I think, or in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The end of 1995 and the beginning of 1996, that is to say, as soon as the indictment appeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that at first you did not take the indictment seriously because you thought that it could not have been something that serious; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As time went by, you changed your view, didn't you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, it's not that I did not take the indictment seriously. I could not have thought how I would be connected to this indictment. I could not believe that I was the one who was in the indictment. I thought that it was some kind of a mistake or something like that. That's what I meant when I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, for two years, you lived in great uncertainty, and finally you surrendered yourself to the court. Tell me, why did you not surrender yourself earlier, since you did things connected to surrender, you wrote to people you thought you should write to in this connection?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: During those two years, we wrote to various addresses and we contacted various people. We wanted to talk about this, and we said that we were available for such discussions, that we wanted to see what was going on. We were available to discuss this. We are small people. We did not know how to get here. We tried to do our best. It was very dangerous to live under such circumstances. Everybody tried to take advantage of you. Of course we were afraid. I said we were small; we did not know how to do this and how to report here and how to come here. That is the main reason why we remained for that year and a half waiting to come here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us, in conclusion, the Prosecutor asked you something very similar, and I'm going to put the same question to you. After having been here for two years, and after having participated in this trial for two years, and after having listened for a year, and after having listened to all these witnesses, what is your reaction to all of this, and how have you been living through all of this, you and your family?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can say that four years of my life have been totally ruined. It is only God who gives me the strength to endure that which I endured during those first two years and that which I have been enduring for these past two years. I never feared coming here. From the very outset, I tried to come here and to prove my innocence. Under such circumstances, in Vitez, I did not hide at all. I lived in Vitez throughout, although it was very dangerous. My family was traumatised. My son, Marko, is receiving assistance from a psychologist now. He is the only child in Vitez to be receiving assistance from a child psychologist, and he could not even finish the first grade properly. And my daughter, Marija, she stutters, and these are major traumas. My child, Marko, he is invariably afraid of SFOR, and both of them wear glasses, and they have to change their glasses every two months. These are major expenses, and my wife doesn't have a job, and my family needs me. My mother is the only mother in the world who has two war criminals. The media never said "suspects;" they invariably say "war criminals." This is a terrible blemish which perhaps we will never be able to rid our name of. I never wished any evil on anyone, let alone my neighbours. I was brought up in a Christian way. My mother did her best to bring us up properly. I was simply born there. I lived there. I lived there through no choice of my own. I did not have any choice. I'm absolutely not guilty. I had nothing to do with this crime. Had somebody else been in my place on that day, perhaps he would have been more courageous than me; perhaps he would have done something. But I could not have done anything. I could not have saved anyone. The only things I did are the things I told you about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. Mr. Kupreskic, I would have a few questions for you, but you look tired. If you would prefer, I can refrain from asking questions. Tell me. I don't want to -- to torture you. Would you be prepared to answer questions, or would you like to have a rest now, and to retire? And I should add that of course, your mother is right, you are not a war criminal, it goes without saying. You are only accused, and you enjoy a very fundamental right, namely, the presumption of innocence. The Court is there exactly to deal with this matter. Well, if you don't refuse to answer this question, I'll tell you, Mr. Kupreskic, there is one matter which troubles me a lot, and this is the testimony of that little girl, Witness H, you know, who was 13. Now, you deny having met that girl on the 16th of April, 1993, but she said here in court that she saw you, you know where, and you know what she said, I mean, because you were here in court. She said that actually she saw you with a weapon, and she knelt down in front of you and asked you to save her life. And actually she is not accusing you of murder, of killing. She is saying that actually, you didn't do anything. You didn't shoot, you didn't kill her. Actually, she is alive; she came here. So I wonder why she should have lied. Do you have an explanation? Can you think of any reason why she should have said all that here in court about your behaviour that day, the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only reason I can find, I said that these pressures and these agreements that were reached in the end, when they were trying to find who had done this, everybody tried to get names, and names were unknown. These combinations were made, and it was said that shooting came from our houses. That is the only thing I can connect it to. I do not see any other reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kupreskic. Thank you so much, also, for giving evidence in court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, after the testimony of the Kupreskic brothers, Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac and I would like to make a proposal, namely, these days, the Prosecutor of this court stayed in Zagreb and talked to the Croatian Minister of Justice, and during that visit, the following topic was raised, that some accused could be released and could defend themselves freely. I believe that we have firmly proven before this Court that the Kupreskic brothers are not so-called warlords, and they did not take part in any political decision-making that led to a Croat-Muslim war, and evidence with regard to some of the other counts in the indictment of the Prosecutor will be assessed. We would kindly ask the Court, in view of the fact that this trial has been going on for so long, and in view of the fact that there will be a recess in the court, and also in this trial, for about two months, and bearing in mind the specific qualities of the two accused -- and I shall not elaborate on that now, because this will be referred to in the closing arguments -- we kindly ask the Trial Chamber to look into the possibility of releasing the accused provisionally. Of course, the Trial Chamber can present the conditions for this, perhaps giving bail, or something, which would be a guarantee that the accused would come back for the continuation of their trial. Of course they will be put at the disposal of this Court if the Court wants them back in the detention unit. We don't want the Prosecutor to state his views right now, but could he please consult the Prosecutor, Ms. Arbour? And we think that if anyone could defend themselves from freedom, we think that it is our clients, honestly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Counsel Radovic. You know, of course, that we have a Rule, Rule 65, on provisional release. Under this Rule, release may be ordered by a Trial Chamber only in exceptional circumstances, after hearing the host country, and only if it is satisfied that the accused will appear for trial, and if released, will not pose a danger to any victim, witness, or other person. Now, under this Rule, it is for you to file a motion to the Trial Chamber, and then we will of course request also the Prosecution to comment on your motion, and we will duly decide on the motion. All right. So we now may release Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic. Again, thank you, Mr. Kupreskic. Yes, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, I would just like to tender into evidence D115/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. No objection? All right. It is admitted into evidence. Counsel Radovic? (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, today I decided on this oral presentation because a ruling was passed that oral presentations could be made in applications, rather than submissions in writing, in order to expedite proceedings. Of course, if you wish, it is no problem for me to present this in writing as well, so it is really up to you to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. You're right. Of course, we decided, in agreement with the President and at the request of the registrar, to try to prompt parties to make oral presentations, oral motions, so as to avoid wasting time and having a lot of paperwork. However, I, for one, would feel that in this particular case, you would have to set out the special reasons which, in your view, would justify the provisional release of the two accused. As I said before, under Rule 65, there must be exceptional circumstances, so it would be for you to prove what particular exceptional circumstances would warrant the provisional release of the accused in question. So therefore, I would think it will be proper for you to file a written motion. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But, of course, this could be filed at right away, I mean, today, and we promise that we would ask the Prosecution to submit, maybe, oral argument -- I mean, I wonder whether you could, to save time, whether you could try to respond orally, because I do understand why Counsel Radovic is very keen to request the Trial Chamber to pass on this matter as soon as possible. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we're quite ready to answer verbally, tomorrow, if you wish, or perhaps even now. But as you have said, we are needing to comply with Rule 65 of the Rules and not some other statements which we read about in the press. Counsel Radovic and Counsel Slokovic-Glumac need to inform the Trial Chamber about those exceptional circumstances before the decision is taken. So far, I have not heard from Mr. Radovic about any exceptional circumstances. All I heard is that we shall have a two-month interruption. I heard about that, but nothing apart from that, nothing that would indicate that there are any exceptional circumstances. So I'm at your disposal fully, of course. I shall be quite ready to respond whenever the Trial Chamber wishes me to do so. But we have not heard any argument presented to support this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, quite, and that is why I asked Mr. Radovic to put down in writing those exceptional circumstances which would be justifying our decision on their possible provisional release. Mr. Radovic, will you please put down on paper the list of all these reasons, and then we can decide on that. Mr. Radovic, do you wish the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot do it today because I need to draft it well and then have it translated, but I will have it tomorrow, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder if we should take a break now, and then -- yes, now. All right, so we'll take a break now, a 30-minute break, and then when we resume our hearing, I think Counsel Krajina will call, I assume, Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic? Good. So that we can probably finish by tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We'll take a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic, good morning. Would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Krajina:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you ready to testify today?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please state your full name for the transcript, your date of birth, and your residence?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: My name is Vlatko Kupreskic. My father's name is Franjo, mother of Marija, born Jonjic. I was born on 1 January, 1958 in the elementary school building in Ahmici, in Pirici, in the municipality of Vitez, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I have lived in Pirici all my life, that is, in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe your family a little bit for us? What were the circumstances of your family?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I come from a multi-ethnic family. My cousin Zdenka Jonjic, who was uncle's daughter, married a Muslim, Nusret Bajric in Zenica. My other cousin, whose name is Marija Kupreskic and is my uncle's daughter, married a Serb, Cedo Lalic. My own sister, Jelina, also married a Muslim in Travnik, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please give us some very brief description of your life up until now?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Let me just describe my family further. I was born in the elementary school in Ahmici. He had seven children altogether, so we were a family of nine. My older brother died, he had a heart condition, and also one of my sisters died. I myself also was born with a heart condition, congenital heart condition, and I am now the only male sibling. I have four sisters. I married Ljubica Kupreskic, and I have a daughter Milena who was born in 1982. I have a son Igor who was born in 1986. In 1993, I had semi-grown-up children. In April 1993, my daughter was fully 11 and my son, Igor, was fully 7 years of age. When I said that I also took care of the family, that means that I also took care of my parents because they were left without any incomes in 1989, and I continue to financially support them to date. I should also point out that I also financially supported an elderly woman who was without and childless. She was alone in the village. I took her into my house and adapted the house for her use. She lived with us for 18 years until she died, and then I also put a gravestone on her grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of schools did you go to?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I went to a school in Ahmici, then another four years in Dubravica. Then I went to Travnik for the secondary school training, and then I went and studied economy, and I graduated in Sarajevo in 1981 as an economist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now briefly describe how your professional career evolved after you graduated?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: After I graduated, I had a scholarship from the SPS, and so seven days after my graduation, I started working for that company in Vitez, and I worked there until 1991. But I want to point out that in 1983, I also worked as a teacher. I taught economics in the secondary school in Vitez. Then I also played music. This is something that I did in my secondary school and during my studies, and I supported my studies, my own studies and the studies of my sisters, by playing music. Then I went to work for the SPS. I went into the investments department, and after about four months, I was promoted to the position of manager in this department. I think that I stayed in this job until about 1988. It may be interesting to point out that I was involved in the two largest investments of this company with the Czech Republic and the USSR for rocket fuel and another one with a company in Dallas, Texas, so I successfully completed those two investment transactions. Then I wanted to move on and ahead, and I went into the finance department where I stayed until about September of 1991, and then of my own will, I left the company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will come back to that at some point. But you said that you had a congenital heart condition. What has your health condition been and what is it today?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Until I had heart surgery in the military hospital in Belgrade in 1966, the physicians predicted that I may die, just like my two other siblings did, in other words, my condition was not very good. But following this surgery, it improved, but it is not perfect to date. Because it is a congenital condition, I must not undergo much stress and I need to avoid conflictual situations. I have perspirations occasionally, and these are some of the symptoms that still persist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to take you to the period of 1991/1992. This was the period when the first democratic elections took place and the establishment of the HDZ and the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What did you do at that time? What type of activities were you involved in?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was with the SPS company in the financial department, and I was the head of the finance department. The economic crisis had deepened by that time, there was a recession, and the HDZ was established in the Republic of Croatia. However, I saw that the problems were growing in this company, that it was very difficult to go on working, that there was less and less money around, that the responsibilities were growing, and I had no interest in staying there, so I made a decision to leave it, and this took place sometime around September 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left the company, what did you do, when you left the SPS company?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: After leaving the SPS company, I think I did not work anywhere for about two months, and then Ivica Kupreskic, my cousin, invited me to work with him in his company, since I had some economic expertise and he had nobody of that profile. So sometime in November 1991, I moved to the company which was called Stefani-Bosna. I later reregistered it myself and renamed it Sutre. As I was used to working and working in my field, and sometimes also I was involved in music, in addition, for awhile, temporarily I worked at the police station. The head of the police at that time, Mirko Samija, asked me to compile an inventory at the police station, and this was in the latter part of December 1992, and I was involved in that until about 25 February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you now tell me, after these ethnic-based parties were established, what was your position in relation to them, and how did you relate to the creation of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I travelled a lot. I moved around a lot. I followed the media, and I saw that in the Republic of Croatia, when the ethnic-based HDZ party won, it took over the power. And as we all know, shortly thereafter, the war broke out. Even then I had a negative position against the ethnic-based parties, and even to date I view them in a negative way, and I was proven right, later, that they all lead to war. All I could see was that this was going to lead to war. This was another reason why I left the company. These were great responsibilities. I thought that I would run into problems with certain regulations. I did not want to be sanctioned by anyone, because I was never criminally involved in anything. I did not want to be in a position to have to violate any laws.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly, how did you interpret these events and the rise of the ethnic-based parties? What were the goals of these parties, and of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: To me, these events meant turmoil and danger because in Bosnia and Herzegovina, three ethnic-based parties emerged, each representing one ethnic group and pursuing their interests exclusively. I never could justify that, but this is what happened. These ethnic-based parties won. They took over the power in their own territories. First they took over executive, then later on military power, and then soon serious problems developed from that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you have just told us, what would you say? Did you support their goals?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I've told you, ever since the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, my attitude was completely negative towards all of them, the HDZ, SDA, and SDS. You saw what happened in Bosnia. After 40 years of political blindness in the former Yugoslavia, all of a sudden those political parties emerged overnight, and people were not used to that, especially to national -- to ethnic parties. We live in Bosnia, and I told you that my family is a multi-ethnic one, and I was fully aware that it was impossible to reach an agreement. It was impossible to achieve peace. Don't you see how, to this day, we have problems down there, and I don't think we shall be able to get rid of these problems until we get rid of ethnic parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, at that time, in any way whatsoever, were you politically active?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, never, in any way whatsoever, was I politically active. Nobody even offered me, neither my Muslim neighbours nor my Croat neighbours, and I do not think that anyone said this. I never even came near a meeting, let alone attended a meeting, precisely because I did not really think much of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that at the time that we are talking about, you were in your private business, that is, first in Ivica Kupreskic's company and then that you founded your own company. That is so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now tell us briefly, what did Ivica Kupreskic's company do, and what was your specific duty there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Sutre company was a trading company and nothing else, throughout that time -- that is, before the war and even, in part, during the war and after the war -- and it mostly traded in foodstuffs or, rather, consumer goods and foodstuffs for the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do in that company?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I was a professional there. I was mostly in charge of documentation, and I also dealt with all the commercial deals because I had tremendous experience in negotiating about special-purpose equipment while I still worked for the SPS -- again, while I still worked for the SPS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this company procure for the army or for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, our company never purchased anything, either foodstuffs or anything else, for the military. It was impossible at the time, because the army had its own logistics, and they had their own procurement bases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, please, on what terms were you with your cousins, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic? I mean privately, on what terms were you with them? Did you often see one another? Did you call on one another? Will you please tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, we were always on good terms. Naturally, we were related, and we called on one another. But as I really was very busy -- at times, I would work at three places in one day -- even my own people, my own household family members saw me rarely, let alone others. But we did, of course, go to one another's houses. That was the tradition, that was the custom, at annual holidays, we would do, such as Christmas, Easter, birthdays, somebody's death, and suchlike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mirjan and Zoran, what did they do at that time? I'm asking you that because the indictment claims that, together with the two of them, you were a member of the HVO, and that you had a joint company with Zoran Kupreskic. What will you say to that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: That is not true. Zoran Kupreskic never worked in our company. His profession is completely different, and I don't mean this as an offence, but he is absolutely contraindicated for any kind of trade. He has no gift whatsoever for that. And as for me, I was never a member of the HVO. I have been relieved of military duty because I'm 100 per cent disabled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Will you now tell us, at that time, that is, 1991, 1992, on what terms were you with your Muslim neighbours or your business partners who were Muslims? Could you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, since I was brought up in that kind of family, so that since my earliest childhood, I was on very good terms with my Muslim neighbours and everybody else, and all other people. Very good terms. All the more so as I had -- and that was the only shop -- I mean, in the Muslim part of the village, mine was the only shop there. And if nothing else, I was bound to be interested in maintaining good terms with everybody. There is also documentation to that effect, but we do not wish to burden this Court with that. I would give merchandise on tick, not only to my Muslim neighbours, but to Muslims and Serbs throughout Central Bosnia. When the war broke out, I must say that I had considerable claims on all of them. And after the war ended, I continued to do business in the same way, even with my Muslim neighbours and with everybody else, with all other people, regardless of their ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your good relations with Muslims, did they change, rather, did they deteriorate at some intervals of time, or were they always the same level -- I mean, during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, that period of time, until practically on the 16th of April, 1993, these relations between us did not change or, rather, they did not deteriorate, because my behaviour, my attitude, my conduct, never gave any reason to them to change their attitude to me. In particular, I had no reason to change my attitude to them because I wasn't in anything. I did not take part in anything. Let me give you just one information. I never hoisted a flag on my shop, even though it was my duty to do so. But I was very careful so as not to, in a manner, undermine my trustworthiness, my authenticity, and my relations with Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let us try to be more specific. On what terms were you with Pezers, who were your neighbours? Will you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, as with all the other neighbours. The relations were outstanding, and that includes the Pezer family. His two younger daughters regularly were with my sisters, and until the very last day, that is, the 16th of April, all the neighbours would greet me every time, and my whole family. My mother, since Fata Pezer was a sick woman, an ill woman, she would always go to take her offerings. I also went there to take her rice and chicken meat, because I think she was a diabetic, so that she needed special food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your relations with Sakib Ahmic and his family?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: As for Sakib Ahmic, he is my father's generation, and they paid calls on one another, and they socialised. Yes, they did have some problems about that boundary, but believe me, he was in trouble about that boundary with everybody, because to the south he bounded on Croat property and on the other side on the Muslim property, and there was no neighbour with whom he hadn't got into some trouble. I mean, he was really a short-tempered man, and even his own children had trouble with him. But I didn't have any trouble with him, and I never bore any grudge against him. I was on particularly good terms with his children because his children were quite good people, and they embraced modern ideas, a modern way of thinking, like I did, so that we were on really good terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kupreskic. Let us now go to the 20th of October, 1992, that is, the time of the first conflict, as we call it here, the first conflict between Muslims and Croats. Could you please tell us, what do you know about that conflict? Where were you on that day, on the 20th of October, 1992, and will you briefly tell us what you remember about that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of October, 1992 -- that means the night before, the eve of that -- I was sleeping. I was asleep at home. My family, we were all there. Early in the morning we were woken up by a detonation, and we got up, tried to see what was going on, what it was all about. But after that, no gunfire, no shooting ensued, so that we could hear nothing or see nothing, but we nevertheless went down to the garage, which is in the lower part of my house. After that, the gunfire started around 8.00 or 9.00, the gunfire began, and we were in this garage. Around 10.00 or 11.00, as there were two small windows just to let air in, I could see an occasional neighbour, a Muslim, from the lower village, how they would move or, rather, how they were fleeing towards the upper part of the village. After that, the gunfire stopped, and there was no more gunfire. But then around 2.00 or 3.00, the Muslim neighbours who lived in the lower part and down by the main road, near the cemetery, they began passing by my house, and I remember quite well the Zec family. I also remember Mujo Ahmic's family, and he was my school fellow or, rather, his father, who was even leading a cow. I went out to ask what it was all about, because I didn't know anything, and they told me that their houses were under gunfire and that they had left their houses. After that, the gunfire continued, and we dispersed, that is, we parted company, rather. I went to the garage, and they went on towards the village, and that is how the day ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, will you tell us, what do you think of that event of the 20th of October? What did you think of it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Later on, at the time when there was no gunfire, I tried, of course, to find out what was going on, so I called my cousin Ivica. I thought that perhaps he had managed to get to the company premises, but I didn't find him there, he was at home, and he seemed to be better informed and told me that it was a clash between two armies at a checkpoint near the cemetery. As I learned that it was a clash between two armies, of course, I was worried about that, but after that, I heard that none of our neighbours had taken part in it and it encouraged me, in a way. But, naturally, when I heard that men had been killed, both a Muslim and a Croat had been killed, then, of course, I took a negative attitude to that event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that event of the 20th of October, 1992, did you expect any new conflicts between Croats and Muslims? Did the relations aggravate between them?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: As for the relations in the village of Ahmici, after that, I did not notice any deterioration. I'm saying, as far as I was informed, all my neighbours regularly came to my shop, and everybody greeted my family regularly on the road until that day, until the 16th of April, 1993. But when one travelled through Central Bosnia through checkpoints and roadblocks, I could see that the situation was growing more complex, because at those roadblocks, the first thing I could see there was that their number was increasing and that they were manned by ever more people and that those people manning the barricades were ever better armed. Also from the media, especially as to the events in east and west Bosnia, this situation was getting more complex.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your behaviour and your attitude change after that event?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, I absolutely did not change my attitude, particularly to my neighbours, because I did not take any part whatsoever in the first conflict. There was no reason for it. So we just resumed normal life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, at that time or perhaps a little bit earlier, village guards were organised, and we heard a great deal about that here and I do not want to ask you to tell us exactly about that, but will you please tell me if you took part in mounting those guards?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, I never took part in this guard duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But weren't you asked to join those guards, and what can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a meeting with Zoran Kupreskic once, and he told me that they intended or they were intending on mounting those guards, and I said that I respected their intentions and that I appreciated their opinion as regards those guards but that I did not want to participate in that and that I would be very happy if they respected my decision, and that's what happened. Because Zoran knows that I never served in the army, I was not trained to use weapons, and I had no time for that because I was busy.
