I told you I worked at two places at once practically, and, besides, I was the only member of my family -- I was the patriarch, so I was the one who was the provider for the whole family, the only one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now we are moving on to the time of the eve of the conflict which took place on the 16th of April, 1993, and I should like us to focus on the days immediately preceding the conflict, that is, the 14th and the 15th of April, 1993. Could you tell us, briefly tell us, exactly where were you on those days and what did you do on those days?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I was regularly working for my company. However, on the 14th, in the evening, Ivica's wife, Ankica Kupreskic, was to arrive from Germany. She had been in Germany for more than a year. Then Ivica and I agreed, naturally, to go and fetch her but also to seize that opportunity and do it also as a kind of a business trip so as to negotiate and bring in some merchandise, and that's how it was. We wrote the order for the business trip on the 13th of April, but on the basis of that travel order, we could not move about, and we needed to get such a permit from the army, from the HVO. We were issued that travel permit on the 14th of April, 1993, and that morning, on the 14th of April, early in the morning, we left to Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you travel and which way did you go? Which road did you take and what time did you leave?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We left on the 14th of April, 1993, early in the morning. I think it was 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning. We took Ivica's Yugo 45 car, and we set off from Vitez via Novi Travnik, Metkovic, to Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Split, at what time approximately, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, let me just mention one thing, one thing that is very important: En route to the border crossing at Metkovic, at Pocitelj, we met a person who testified here before this Court on the 6th of May, 1999 under the pseudonym Witness DE, that is to say, that we encountered that person on the 14th of April, 1993 in the town of Pocitelj. Then we proceeded to the Metkovic border crossing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Did you spend some time there with this person, and what was this person doing? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: At this gasoline station, we were buying fuel, and that's where we met this person. We spent about 15 minutes there with him. We talked about some very basic matters. We said where we were going and we were asking him where he was coming from, and he said that he was coming from Split, and we saw his truck where there had been a lot of big packages, and we didn't really discuss anything else. Then we moved to Metkovic, to the border crossing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Then we came to Split, approximately around 12.00, because we were supposed to see someone at the Koteks company. We were supposed to purchase some salt there. Then we bought some textile goods. We did all of that. We put it into the car and we went to the Split airport, which is about 15 kilometres away from the town of Split, and in the evening, around 9.00 p.m., that is where we met Ivica Kupreskic's wife, Ankica Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do you remember what kind of goods were concerned, and how much did you have?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, we wanted to cover the costs of the trip, so we got some blue jeans, Levi's, 501s, and then we also obtained some underwear and 20 pairs of sneakers for children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said that you met Ankica. Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Since it was late, we left the airport and proceeded to Baska Voda. We came to Baska Voda to our friend Radoslav Simovic's place, and that's where we spent the night. We spent the night after the 14th of April there. In the morning of the 15th of April, 1993, early in the morning, I think around 6.00, we set out for Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who was travelling, the three of you; right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ivica, his wife Ankica, and I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you arrive home approximately?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, we arrived home rather late. The road via Mostar had been closed, so we were told to take a different road, so we had to make a longer trip via Mount Vran, and we arrived home on the 15th of April, 1993, around 7.00 p.m. We arrived in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: First when we arrived, we unloaded these textiles and our other goods in the garage. Then Ankica and Ivica said that they wanted to go to Ankica's family in Krcevina, so after we unloaded the goods, they left and I remained home with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go out somewhere that evening?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: That evening, I did not go out at all because I was very tired, and, on the other hand, we also had to prepare the goods for our buyer from Travnik. That is the kind of agreement that we had reached, that on the next day, the 16th of April, 1993, by 8.00, I'd send the goods to the buyer. We were packing these goods, we were preparing the bills, et cetera, so we did not leave the house at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. When you returned from Split, when you returned home on the evening of the 15th of April, did you see any soldiers by your house and by your shop when you arrived back from Split?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: When the three of us returned from Split, I did not see any soldiers, either in the shop or in the house or in front of the house. The shop was open until 6.00 p.m. and then it was closed, and in the house and around the house, absolutely not, I did not see any soldiers, nor did my wife tell me about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So things looked usual, did they?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Everything was normal and usual, just like any other day. I could not notice any difference, even more so because I had asked the children how things went at school. At that time, they attended school regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, in your interview with the Prosecutor of the Tribunal, you said that you went to Split on the 13th of April, 1993 and that you spent the night in Split at a lady's place. Please, how do you explain that? How do you explain the difference between that statement that you made to the Prosecutor and what you are saying about it today?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how I explain it: When I made that statement, in front of me was, like today, so you can have a look at this, I had this travel order for a business trip. In the upper corner, there was this date of the 13th of April, 1993. So that is a travel order of the Sutre company, and then when I talked about that part, and you can listen to the cassette too, I did not think that this was an important piece of information. Now I am saying with full responsibility that we left on this trip on the 14th of April, 1993 because we could not get out of Vitez at -- we could not pass the checkpoint with this order only; we could only have a military order too in order to get out. So it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So it was a slip of the tongue that you made; right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the interview had been taking place for quite some time, and I was quite tired as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let us move on to the actual date of the conflict, and that is the 16th of April, 1993. Please, could you try, as precisely and as briefly as possible, to say what you did on that day, what you experienced on that day, what you did, and who you were with.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to mention that when I arrived on the 15th of April, 1993, in the evening, I informed this person, whose pseudonym is DF, that on the next day, by the morning hours, I would bring him the required goods. After having packed the goods and after having prepared the bills, we went to bed. I slept until 5.00. I did not wake up at all because I was really very tired. But around 5.00 in the morning, my wife, Ljubica, woke me up, and she said that I should answer the phone, which is what I did. When I answered the phone, an unknown voice said to me, "Vlatko, what are you waiting for? Go to the shelter." And this person hung up. I did not take this seriously because, even until then, there had been similar situations. So as I was so tired, I went back to bed. However, only a few minutes later, the phone rang again. My wife Ljubica answered the phone again and said that Ivica was calling. I answered the phone, and Ivica said to me, "Vlatko, what are you waiting for? Go to the shelter. Everybody's already left." And he hung up. After that, I really got worried. I realised that something was wrong. I was particularly confused by what he had said, that everybody had left, and also I wondered why he had hung up immediately. After that, my wife, Ljubica, said to me, "Well, something really must be wrong because somebody called last night around 3.00. I didn't want to wake you up because I know you're tired." Then we realised that we had to go to the shelter very quickly, which is exactly what we did. I went downstairs to my parents, I informed them, and after that, I went to help with the children, and we went downstairs to pick up my parents. However, my mother was ready but my father said, "Vlatko, I'm an elderly man. I don't want to go." At that point in time, the first thing that I thought of doing was to go to Ivica Kupreskic's house to see what was going on, so we proceeded to Ivica Kupreskic's house --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. So who left?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: My wife, my two children, my mother, and I, the five of us. When we arrived at Ivica Kupreskic's house, we did not find anyone there, we did not see anyone there, and, therefore, we panicked even more. So we left quickly in the direction of the forest. We passed through the forest, and we came to the house of Niko Sakic, and about 50 metres after that is an asphalt road. In the yard in front of Niko Sakic's house, we met Niko Sakic, and on the right-hand side, also in the yard of the house of Dragan Samija, we met Dragan Samija. We proceeded further down towards the shelter, and about 50 metres after that point, we met Milan Samija and his wife Mara Samija. We proceeded further towards the shelter until we came to the end of the sports grounds in Zume, and then we heard terrible detonations, strong detonations, that is to say, that it is heavy fire that was heard first, shells, and we were terrified, and we hurried towards the shelter even faster. When we arrived in front of the shelter, we found a few people there. I know that I saw Ivo Vidovic and I know that I saw Jozo Vrebac. Then we went into the shelter and went downstairs to the lower floor of that shelter, and we all stayed in a room that was on the left-hand side, that is to say, to the left of the staircase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We shall continue, but could you please clarify another point for us? Why did you go to the shelter of Jozo Vrebac specifically?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: When the first shelling of Vitez and Busovaca took place by the aircraft of the Yugoslav People's Army, we sought shelter there. That was actually a house that, in our opinion, was the safest place for us to seek shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went there earlier; right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just another additional question. On the way between your house and the shelter, did you encounter any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not see anyone?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No. No, we did not see any soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now you're in the shelter. Approximately when did you arrive at the shelter? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Later on, and I also heard about this here, I was the last one to get out there to the shelter, so we must have arrived around 6.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how much time did you spend in the shelter? Until when did you stay in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I stayed in the shelter until approximately 10.00. There was intensive shooting. Although we were inside, the shooting could, indeed, be heard. I really became nervous. I heard all this shooting and I realised that this was a conflict, so I was really troubled. I even had a guilty conscience. I wanted to go and see what was happening to my father because he had remained at home. So I kept thinking how, but the shooting was still so intense. But around 9.30 or 10.00, I had a feeling that the shooting had subsided a bit. Even earlier, I had proposed to my wife, Ljubica, that I go out and try to see what was going on with my father; however, she had opposed that. She said, "That's impossible. You're going to get killed." However, later, I said at one point, when I simply couldn't take it any longer, I said, "Ljubica, I have to go. It seems to me that there are people who are wounded there, and I have to go and help the wounded." So I simply went out of the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you say this about wounded people? Why did you tell your wife that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, at that point in time, it occurred to me because I thought that, in that way, I'm going to pacify her and convince her of what I'm supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: So when I got out to the road by this shelter, I saw Jozo Vrebac. He said, "Where are you going?" And I said, "Jozo, it's almost 10.00. I have to see my father." So I just went on, and that is how I took shortcuts. I was hiding, so I didn't take the main road where there was shooting, so I went from one point where I would feel protected to another. I came to the forest that was about 50 metres in front of Niko Sakic's house. When I got out of this forest, that is to say, when I reached the area where Niko Sakic's house was, Niko Sakic caught sight of me and said, "Vlatko, run this way." Since I noticed him too, I ran towards him, and he took me directly to his doorway and we went into his kitchen. As the shooting went on continuously, I was in Niko Sakic's kitchen with him expecting to see whether I would get an opportunity to go over to my house. But when I came close, I saw that around my house, there was terrible shooting going on in that area. He asked me, "What are you doing here? Where are you going?" And I said that I was going to see what happened to my father because he stayed in the house, and I said, "Well, Niko, do you know what is going on here? What is happening? This is a real war here." And he said, "Vlatko, I don't know, but this morning I saw some HVO soldiers going in the direction of your house." So I stayed in this kitchen sometime until perhaps 12.30, I don't know, but I know that in that period of time, the shooting died down, sometime after 12.00. In fact, around 12.30, there was no more shooting, so I concluded that if there is no shooting, there is no shooting at all and there hasn't been any for the last 15 minutes, I thought that perhaps I could go home because there was no shooting. I thought that it had stopped. As I felt pressured to see what had happened to my father, I just left Niko Sakic's house and started out alongside the lower edge of the forest towards the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina, may I suggest that we take a 15-minute break? Is it fine? Because we will go on until 1.30. Good. 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before asking Counsel Krajina to resume with the examination-in-chief, I would like to report on a decision we have made over the coffee break. On reflection, we thought that Counsel Radovic could probably submit his motion orally tomorrow morning. We thought we should speed up matters and avoid red tape. So in spite of what we had said before, I think it's better for you, if you wish to do so, to avoid writing a motion, filing a motion, and you could set out all the various reasons, so we will use the transcript of your oral motion as a sort of document on which we will base ourselves. And of course we would then immediately ask the Prosecutor, if possible, to react and to say whether or not he objects to your motion. This could be done tomorrow morning, maybe first thing tomorrow morning, if this is suitable. All right? Good. So we -- yes, Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, then, as you just suggested, I am going to submit my arguments for the motion for provisional release tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, let's resume. Are you ready, sir? We left off at the point where you came to Niko Sakic's house. Please go on with your account now.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: So I left Niko Sakic's house, and I passed the garage, skirting the lower edge of the forest towards my house. So I arrived at this road leading towards Zoran and Ivica Kupreskic's houses, and then from there continued on towards my old house. When I arrived in the area between my shed and the old house, I could see the entrance to the new house, and I looked at the first floor. At that entrance, by the facade, against the facade, I saw a soldier who was moving around, and I saw that he was observing the southern and northern sides. I was surprised, and I raised my arms, and I said "I am Vlatko Kupreskic." He noticed me. He trained his rifle on me, and he said, "What do you want?" And I said, "I live in this house. I came to get my father." He said, "Approach." I approached. I came to the entrance, and he said, "Follow me." We went upstairs to the first floor, the top floor of my house. He led the way; I followed. He first entered the hallway, because from the hallway, on the right-hand side, there are two good-sized rooms, and he opened the door to the first, and he said, "This one came to get his father." When I entered, in both of these rooms, there were a number of soldiers; I believe somewhere around seven or eight soldiers. At the table, I saw my father; he was sitting in a chair. I approached him. I hugged him. He started crying and whispered in my ear, "Vlatko, calm down," because I was shaking. I had been frightened. So I sat down. I was still scared. I looked around at these men, the soldiers, and avoided their eyes at the same time. I was afraid that I or my father might be killed. And even downstairs, as I was entering the house, the door had been broken in, and the door upstairs almost was not around. Everything had been ransacked. The merchandise which I had arranged was all thrown around. The soil which was in the flowerpots, that earth, that soil, had been spilled around the carpeting. So everything was completely turned upside down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on we will come back to that period when you were in the house, but now just tell me, how long did you spend in the house, and then where did you go? Where did you go afterwards?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It seemed so long to me, because I didn't dare ask or say anything. I kept silent. But at that moment, one of the soldiers was using a Motorola to communicate with someone, and a couple of moments later, somebody said, he said, "Attack." They all fell to the ground, and my father and I stayed in our chairs. Then one of them pulled me down to the ground too. I didn't know why, but after a while, I heard the sound of tanks. One of them made a couple of movements and raised his head a little bit. Because the door of my balcony was almost all glass, he peeked out, and he said, "They're coming towards us." So we were on this floor, but the tanks did not stop. They just went by my store and went towards the school building. Just judging by the noise, when they were somewhere around the school building, one of them said, "Get up." They all got up. I kept silent, but I was upset and angry. It is hard for me to describe this. One of them seemed to have noticed that. Later on, it turned out that they had completely robbed and looted the house. So one of them said to me, "Come over here," and he took me down through the same hallway to the small terrace near the entrance, and "What do you want?" he said. "Is this what you would want?" And he pointed at the house of Suhreta Ahmic, which was on fire. I just kept silent, because now I was even more scared. Then he said, "Scram. Come and get your father later." So I quickly ran downstairs, and again using the same path between the shed and the old house, went back to Niko Sakic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Will you now describe what your movements after that were?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: When I emerged from this large forest near the smaller forest, I met Drago Grgic, and another soldier in camouflage uniform, and Anto Vidovic, whose nickname was Satko. Drago asked me, "Vlatko, what are you doing? Where are you coming from?" I said that I had gone to get my father. We stayed there very briefly because the shooting resumed again. We all fled that spot, and myself and Drago Grgic, because Niko Samija was in front of his house, he said, "Come over here." Anto Vidovic, called Satko, and this soldier went on in the direction of the shelter. Later on I learned that in fact Anto Vidovic's family was in the shelter of this Niko Vidovic. So I also went inside Nikola Samija's house, into the basement, where there was a small window, and I stayed there until about 4 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I was still very concerned throughout this time because the shooting was still going on, and then I kept asking myself why was there not -- I understood that it was because of UNPROFOR that the shooting had stopped, but now I was wondering why did the shooting resume. So when the UNPROFOR vehicles had left the village, the combat had resumed. So I was very concerned about the situation and everything that I had seen and experienced, but again, I had the same problem, that I could not go to the shelter to inform my family, to report to my wife and my mother that I was alive and also that my father was alive. Also, in this basement at Nikola Samija's house, I again was looking for an opportunity to go over to the shelter. So sometime around 4.00 p.m., the shooting again subsided, and again I found a way to get over to the shelter, and I informed my mother and my wife that my father was still alive. I did not want to tell them anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We will continue with your movements following that point in time, but I just want to take you back to that period when you went back to your house and you found seven or eight soldiers there. Now, can you be very specific when answering this question? Did you recognise any of the soldiers there? If you can just describe these soldiers, what they were wearing and how they behaved, and did you recognise anyone?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: When I sat down in this chair, even though I was very frightened, I was 20, 30 centimetres, half a metre, one metre away from these people. They all had their faces painted. Most of them were wearing camouflage uniforms, but two of them definitely had black uniforms on, and some of them even had helmets. On their left shoulders, they had ribbons. I remember that very well because I had never seen that before until then. They were all well-armed, and I could not recognise anyone. Those were all persons unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there in your house where those soldiers were, was there any conversation? Did any conversation take place about the shooting, wounding, or anything?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No. It was a very short period. I did not overhear any kind of conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me take you back to the shelter. You said that you went back to the shelter, so how long did you stay there and what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Josip Vrebac's shelter until about 6.00 p.m., when I judged that I could go over to my father's. So I did this, I went over to the house, and I found my father there but no soldiers. There were no soldiers either inside or around the house. He was very scared. He didn't expect me to come to get him. So my father got ready, I took some good from the refrigerator, I put it in a plastic bag, and slowly we went over to Jozo Vrebac's shelter. My father did not move well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He had broken his hip once, and so with crutches, he was able to move, he was able to walk. Around 7.00 or so, we arrived at the shelter, perhaps even 7.30, I don't know, but it took us awhile to get there. I just remember that when my father finally settled down in the shelter, that a terrible explosion could be heard. I again got out of the shelter to see what had happened now, and later on, we learned that this explosion, in fact, was the blowing up of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you now tell me what your father, Franjo, told you about what he experienced on that day, the 16th of April, in his house? What did he see? What went on in Ahmici? Can you say something about that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Of course I can because I talked to him about it and I asked him how he fared on that day, what happened. He said that he would never forget this as long as he lived because that morning, soldiers had burst inside the house. At the start of this big shooting and shelling, he had taken shelter in the bathroom because the bathroom had been sort of dug in. That northern side of the house is completely submerged and it's under the ground. Then the soldiers found him in the bathroom and asked him who he was. He said that he was Franjo Kupreskic, but they did not believe him. In fact, he even had to go around and search for his personal ID and show it to them, and after that, he was left alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything, whether the soldiers had shot from the house?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that they had shot both from the house and from around the house. I myself, later on when I first came inside the house, I saw bullet casings and soil and the black residue from the gun powder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father describe to you what happened to his neighbours, the Pezers? On that day, did he hear anything?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, he saw, I believe it was, Cazim Ahmic's wife. He told me that he helped Cazim to provide assistance to his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way did he assist him?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: When he saw him carrying his wife, he tried to help but the soldiers wouldn't let him. So if my recollection is correct, he somehow asked them to help him, so they gave him permission. He gave him a blanket and an axe, and Cazim then made sort of a stretcher of sorts, an improvised stretcher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But did he tell you anything about the Pezers' predicament, anything of them?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, after the 16th, on the evening of the 16th when you were reunited with your father, Franjo, in this shelter, how long did you stay in this shelter, and where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I stayed in the shelter until the 17th of April, until the evening, until 20.00 or 21.00 when information again reached us from the -- that a kind of a new attack was being expected from a neighbouring Muslim village, so that I believe everybody left the shelter, and so did I with my family, and we went to Donja Rovna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We stayed in Donja Rovna some 10 or 15 days at the most, but since accommodation was very poor, I then moved my family to Vitez, to Niko Kristo's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there with your family?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In Niko Kristo's house, we stayed until -- well, almost until July, and it was only as late as July that we went back to our house in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Kupreskic, let us now move on to another subject. Will you please tell us if you were called up, if you were mobilised, and when, if so? Will you please be very accurate?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, as I'm not able-bodied, but, yes, the military police used to come to Gornja Rovna and control all the males there, and I always carried that military booklet with me, and, besides, my scar is big enough to show them that I'm not really able-bodied to do any military service. So then later on in Vitez, I managed to somehow avoid being mobilised or that kind of commitment. However, sometime in September 1993, even that was of no avail any more, and the military police took me into custody and directly took me to the office. I believe it was called the defence office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Then when I was brought to the defence office, in a room there, I found Witness DA/5, who testified here on the 20th of January, 1999, and Zoran Drmic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they work there? Were they employed there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they worked there. I immediately gave my military booklet to this lady, and she remarked -- that is, I said that I was disabled 100 per cent, and she remarked, "Why are you bringing me those? I mean, who are you bringing me here?" I did not know her before, that was the first time I saw her, but Zoran Drmic I did know from before. And she said, "I don't know what to do with you," and as I had already had problems with my cars before, because I too had a Yugo 45 and I also had a Mercedes 123, which is quite a powerful car, and I had trouble before because they wanted to requisition it, to confiscate it. Then I remembered and I suggested to that person to be a driver, seeing that I had that car. And she said, "Right. Fine," and called somebody by telephone and told me to report to Mr. Bertovic at the Impregnacija, and that is how I went, got my car, and in that car, that is, a Mercedes, white, 123, I went and reported to Mr. Bertovic. I had never been to that man, nor did I know that man before, but I said that this person had sent me, and they must have been in touch, so he assigned me. He told me to report to the outpatient facility in Zume and to become the medical driver at this outpatient unit at Zume, and that is what I did. I went there, I found that medical unit, and I reported to the commander of that unit. It was Mrs. Finka Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: So I was, therefore, mobilised with that medical unit. Not far from that, and I did not know that, there was the command of the so-called 3rd Company, and the commander of that company called me through my boss, Finka Vidovic, and said that I could not drive for the medical unit alone, and then since there was a shortage of both men and cars, I should also be at the disposal of that company. Naturally, I did that and I drove for them, drove the car for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay with the medical corps?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I was the driver with the medical corps until about the 20th of April, 1994, and then I was demobilised verbally, orally, and that was the end of my duty with that medical corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in Ahmici, and what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, we tried straight away, and that is what we did, both Ivica and I, to reanimate the company. We resumed our work at the Sutre company, and I was there until 1995, when I founded with -- my wife and I founded our own company, called Modus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So now let us please move on to a new subject. Will you tell us, when was it that you learned about the indictment, that you were indicted?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I remember that very well. One day, two people I did not know came to my house. One introduced himself as Sliskovic, and the other one said his name was -- I think Matosevic. As my house was my office -- I mean, my house was also my office, and many people came to me; all sorts of people came there. I didn't know what it was all about. They said they came from the information service, from SIS, and they said that they had heard that I had been indicted, and those are the people who were on that first indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a military service of a kind?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I can't say what kind of a service they were. They only used the acronym. They said, "We come from SIS." But what it meant, really, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you see it now, I mean, that communication, that information, that knowledge that you had been charged? What did you do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: How did I see it? How did I feel? Well, at the beginning -- and I'm just now describing only how I felt -- at first I thought it funny, and then strange, because it defies common sense. Me, to be indicted for Ahmici? I, who had absolutely nothing to do with it? I thought somebody was pulling my leg. It's difficult to explain. But then, when I learned from media, both newspapers and television, really heard it with my own ears, then I realised that that was indeed an accusation. It was charges. But still, at that time, I again thought it was a big, a major mistake, a really very big error, and that it would be redressed in no time at all. However, the situation grew more complex, and I eventually realised that it was very serious, and I began to do something for my defence in June 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do? Did you do something -- did you approach somebody, or what?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes. First I communicated to those people who were in that first indictment. I called them. I'd never seen Marinko Katava in my life. I didn't have the slightest who he was. Vlado Santic, I only met him here in the detention unit, but I had heard about him. So I called my relatives. We met. We were all taken aback and wondered what we should do. But then, again, I repeat, I thought that it might bring fruit and we thought it might be a good idea to write letters both to international institutions and individuals who worked in Bosnia and Herzegovina on behalf of the international community. What struck me most was that Stipo Alilovic was in the same indictment, because I knew that man. His wife, Dragica, worked with me, and I knew that the man had left back in 1992, I mean, went abroad. I moved about. As far as I knew, that man never came back down there. I never saw him again there. So I really thought that those letters would bear some fruit. I signed them and sent them, and in all those letters, we wrote the following: That it was a very big mistake, that those indictments were very sudden, that that was an oversight, that there were people who had nothing do with it, that we were ready to cooperate, that we were willing even to report even to The Hague, that we condemned those crimes. And yet we never received a single answer to any one of those letters. I was quite unhappy about that, and my wife and myself, of course, wrote again, personally, on the 23rd of November, we wrote to this Tribunal. We wrote --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, 1997, was it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was 1997. There we described our problems, and yet nobody replied even to that letter, nor any form of co-operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please give us -- how do you explain, why didn't you surrender as was requested, and were you planning, were you intending to surrender? Were you hiding?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I did not turn myself in, I did not come here with these people, for several reasons -- at least, that is how I explain that. First, because I am remarkably innocent. I am not guilty of what I'm being charged with. Secondly, I'm a sick man, and I thought that I will not be able to stand the detention until this is clarified, this is cleared up. The third reason I did not turn myself in is because -- and there were some suggestions to that effect, to surrender, to turn ourselves in to the Republic of Croatia. But knowing the experience of Zlatko Aleksovski and Pero Skopljak, who were detained in the Republic of Croatia, as a sick man, I simply did not dare do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose idea was that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the idea suggested to me by some people from Croatia, some people who came, and at that time already they were preparing the defence. But I simply did not venture -- I did not dare do that at the time. The fourth reason is that I always thought that I would get a reply, that the whole thing would be cleared up. But in view of my legal obligation towards my company, and I had -- on the 31st of December every year, I had to draw up the annual sheet of balance, so that at that time, when those people came to me, I simply could not -- I did not plan to turn myself in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you think of doing that at all?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and Dr. Krajina, you know that I retained you in November 1997, and that we agreed, and that you were the mediator for this letter of November 1997 which was sent through the Tribunal's office in Sarajevo. You know that we agreed that I should surrender in Sarajevo, to the UNPROFOR, sometime in March 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, did you go into hiding? How did you live?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, those people here know that, and I have countless witness -- both the Muslims, my neighbours, and Croats, too -- that I never hid. Everybody was surprised by that, but I'm not guilty of what I'm being accused of. I have nothing to do with it. Those were the only ideas and the truth which guided me. UNPROFOR came regularly to my place, since I have two business units with my company, both in Ahmici and in Vitez, in the centre of the town. Every day people from UNPROFOR came, bought things from me, bought foodstuffs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would they see you personally?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: On that day, on the 17th of December, 1997, that day, we met twice, at around 9.00 and around 5.00 in the afternoon that day, on the 17th of December. That night, between the 17th and 18th, is when I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So will you tell us, as briefly as possible, will you please tell us, will you recount those things about your arrest. Were you hiding, and how did that happen?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought -- I thought -- let me put it that way, that if I manage somehow until March 1997, until -- if anyone is interested and really wants to take me into custody, that they can do it at any given moment, because I was with those people day in and day out. I simply thought that they would ask for my ID, like any other police, and I would simply take my seat in the car and come here. However, this was done in a very brutal way. On that 17th of December, I had some guests, and we were up until midnight. Then we went to sleep, and so these first hours, between 1.00 and half past 1.00 in the morning, we heard some detonations. The house was full of smoke. Chaos. You know, this is first sleep, a heavy sleep, and I thought I was dreaming that it was war again. But then my wife got up first, and she said, "Hey, Vlatko, we've got thieves in the house." And for the first time in my life I had obtained a rifle, because of these thieves, because of burglars, because of robberies in January 1995, and at the request of my wife. She passed the rifle on to me, because I thought that those were burglars. I wanted to fire, but I didn't know how, and that scared me even more, because I didn't know how to fire a bullet from that. Somehow I did fire a bullet or two, and at that moment, through that big balcony door, those men appeared. When I saw those people, when I realised that they were not burglars but that they were people who were super-equipped, I just dropped my rifle in front of them and sat down. I kneeled, raised my arms, and those men really came to me and immediately extended first aid to me on my couch. They behaved very correctly until they turned me over here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of aid? What are you saying? Were you hurt or what?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I can never forget that. I can't really remember -- I believe I fainted at the time, but I came to on the couch, and then I saw that I had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I was wounded in the armpit, in my arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also explained where you got that rifle from; right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you, Mr. Kupreskic, to comment on some evidence and the counts in the indictment that pertain to you. We shall start briefly with the indictment. Are you aware of all the things that you have been indicted for?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of all the things that I have been indicted for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that -- when you first appeared before this Court, you said that you did not plead guilty with regard to any one of the counts, so I would like to ask you for more extensive comments on this, first of all, from the content of the indictment. That is to say, in point 9, it says that you aided and abetted the attacks on the civilians of Ahmici and Santici, that you participated in military training, and that you were arming yourselves. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I was never a soldier. I never had weapons until after the war. I never participated in any military formations or in political events. I did not help or instigate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you evacuated Bosnian Croats the night before the attack on the 16th? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely incorrect, because the night between the 15th and 16th of April, I was asleep, and I did not wake up at all and that goes for my entire family. It is not correct, because I did not move my family away, my own father, and that is telling proof in itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The indictment also says that you organised the HVO soldiers' ammunition and weapons in and around the village of Ahmici/Santici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely incorrect. I have nothing to do with the army. I never had any weapons. I never had any ammunition. I did not participate in this. I never attended a military or political gathering. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Furthermore, that you prepared your home and the homes of your relatives as staging areas and firing locations for the attack on the 16th of April, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely wrong. You could hear also that I was the last one to be woken up and informed on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993. So this is absolutely wrong, that I was even preparing the house of my other Croat neighbours and my own house. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how come the military was in your house?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: The military, according to the statement of my father, and I also on that day, the 16th of April, 1993, I could see for myself that the military had entered the house violently. They barged through the door. They smashed it open. They took hold of my house, and they used it as a strategic point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So what do you think, why is it precisely your house that was occupied in that way, and why were military operations conducted from it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, you've seen it, and we've seen a lot of it here, so I don't have to point it out once again. My house is the last Croat house in that part of Ahmici, the last Croat house. It is the last house, and also it is at the highest point, and it stands out from the other houses. From the house, the soldiers probably had a good vantage point in terms of viewing this entire part of Ahmici. So it was probably strategically a very good point for them, and they took advantage of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Furthermore, in this count of the indictment, it is stated that you concealed from the other residents that an attack was imminent on the 16th of April, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I repeat once again, this is not correct. First of all, I did not evacuate my father, because I was not aware of any conflict or any problems. Secondly, I was the last one to be informed by Ivica Kupreskic, and five hours later, at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, in points 12, 13, and 14 of the indictment, it is mentioned that you, together with Zoran Kupreskic, and we discussed this a bit earlier on, that you, before the war, had a joint company with him and that you were an HVO soldier in Ahmici. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I already said what I have to say. This just shows how this indictment was written, in such haste. I don't know with which objectives in mind, but it is not correct. I never had a company with Zoran and I was never an HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In the part of the indictment, number 1, that is to say, persecution, count 1, in 21, it says, please follow this carefully, that in the period from October 1992 until April 1993, you took part in the persecution of the Bosnian Muslim inhabitants of Santici, Ahmici, and its environs on political, racial, and religious grounds, and that you took part in the deliberate and systematic killing of Bosnian Muslim civilians, in the comprehensive destruction of their homes and property, and the organised detention and expulsion of Bosnian Muslims from Ahmici, Santici, and its environs. So could you please say whether that is correct, and what do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I never participated in or persecuted my Bosnian Muslim neighbours on religious or other grounds. I never killed anyone. I never harmed anyone. I never put anyone's house on fire. I never hurt anyone. I did not take anyone's property or I, through my own actions and behaviour, not at a single point in time could I have indicated such a thing. So I did not take part in such things that are recounted in that part of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In points 12 through 15 of the indictment, we are talking about the Pezer family, it is being mentioned once again, and I would like you to listen to this very carefully. In point 28, it says that before the attack on the 16th of April, 1993, HVO soldiers, armed with automatic rifles, congregated at your house in Ahmici, and when the attack commenced, several HVO units used your residence as a staging area. Other soldiers shot at Bosnian Muslim civilians from your house throughout the attack. Please, briefly, what do you say to this?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. At the time that is mentioned there, notably, the 16th of April, 1993, I was in the shelter of Jozo Vrebac, almost two kilometres away from the place where these events were unfolding. I was not in front of the house or in the house, and I could not, in any way, participate with the soldiers in the killing and wounding of the Pezer family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you listen to me carefully, the question was related to whether soldiers, before the attack that is described here in the indictment, did they congregate in your house? Were there several units there, several HVO units, and did they use your house, et cetera? You already mentioned this, but please --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No. On the 15th of April, there were no soldiers near my house, let alone in the house. That is not correct, and on the day of the 16th of April, I was almost two kilometres away from these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 16th, that is the only thing that is correct there, on the 16th of April, the soldiers were there throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they shooting?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: They were shooting in the house and around the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 30, subparagraph 30, rather, under the same count in the indictment, it says that you, on the 16th of April, 1993, together with HVO soldiers, in front of your house in Ahmici, took part in the wounding of Dzenana Pezer and another woman and in the killing of Fata Pezer. Is that correct, and what do you say to these charges in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: This absolutely is not correct. On that day, at that time, I was not there at all. The first time I came home was around 13.00 on the 16th of April, 1993. I did not shoot, I was not there, I did not kill anyone, and I did not wound anyone. Doesn't this speak for itself, the thing that you said, that I am being accused of the wounding of a woman? The Prosecutor never said who this woman was. Not a single witness here, out of the 14 members of the family who were moving around, said that they had seen such a woman wounded, and this just shows how loose the indictment is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you think then? Who could have been this woman that the indictment mentions, the woman being wounded, and nobody knows who this is? What do you think? Who is this? Who else was wounded then in this situation? You remember, we heard about it here.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Only if such a degree of confusion was created, then only it could look like this witness, the Muslim witness who was wounded on that day, who testified before this Court on the 31st of May, 1995 under the pseudonym CF. Well, you saw that this witness is a Muslim, a victim, and he came here to testify as a Defence witness for me. He is probably that woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Kupreskic, now I would like to ask you to look at some of the evidence that has been presented during the trial before this Court and also to look at some of the witness statements. Let us look at Prosecutor's Exhibit P329.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, could the registrar please have Prosecutor's Exhibit P329 shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had a look at this, Mr. Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is a certificate, isn't it, concerning your alleged participation in the war. Could you please comment on this a bit? Where does this certificate come from and is the information given in it correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: The information given in this certificate is absolutely incorrect. First of all, the time is not correct because I was mobilised only on the 15th of September, 1993. Secondly, the duty that is mentioned here that I performed, it is not correct. I was a driver for the medical corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain how did this certificate come about? This was presented by the Prosecutor, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I never saw this certificate until the Prosecutor presented it, and it is of a dubious nature, to me. I never signed such a document that I was taking this over. I first saw this document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. Please now let us have a look at another document, and then we can probably adjourn for the day, that is, Prosecutor's Exhibit P335.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had a look at this document, Mr. Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've seen it. I've seen it here so many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at number 107, you can see your name. Could you please comment on that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I can comment on this document in the following way: This is a plain list of male persons. It was probably made on this day, the 16th of April, because we heard here that there are some persons on this list who are not military-able men. There are some persons who are not even in the territory of the municipality of Vitez. So I consider this document to be a plain list of male persons who were supposed to be engaged as of the 16th of April until the 27th of April, probably at the front line, or that they should be mobilised. There is another fact that speaks in favour of this even more, and that is that I did not appear in any other document, the following documents that the Prosecutor presented here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you denying what this list says, that is to say, that on the 16th of April, 1993, you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: This is absolutely incorrect. I was not mobilised on that day. I was mobilised only approximately on the 15th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, since I will have another sequence of questions that will follow, and our time is almost up for the day, I suggest that we adjourn for the day. I believe that tomorrow, by the time the break comes, we will have concluded our questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Before we adjourn, however, let me ask the Prosecutor whether the Prosecution is ready to hand in their list of rebuttal witnesses for September, October, whether you have a rough idea. Also, I would like to turn to Counsel Puliselic, Pavkovic, and Susak and ask them to confirm whether or not they have decided about their clients. Is it now for sure that the three accused will not give evidence in court? Again, this is for the purpose of doing some planning for the September hearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This afternoon, Mr. President, we shall submit a document, and it will show what we are planning for this stage. Yes, we do have a rather precise idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask Counsel Puliselic, Pavkovic, and Susak whether it is now for sure that their three clients will not give evidence in court, will not be called by them, just a confirmation. Counsel Puliselic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, not at a single point in time did I say that Papic would not testify. I said that I did not know about this. I think that he will testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So this will be in September then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have already stated my position concerning this matter, so I think I can only reiterate it now, that my client decided not to avail himself of his right to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I also believe that Drago Josipovic, for the time being, has not decided to testify in this particular trial, that he would not testify, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So it's not a question mark; it's a no. So he will not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So the only one who will then testify is Dragan Papic, and this will happen in September when we resume. All right. We will adjourn now until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 23rd day of July, 1999, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
